# From pilot data to a future study

A research team has pilot genotypes from cases and controls and wants to plan
a larger, independent study of the same variant in a comparable population.
The pilot data can estimate the genotype frequencies that a future study
might encounter. `paweh` uses these frequencies to calculate a required sample
size or the power of a proposed design.

This example uses **synthetic data**, with deliberately fixed genotype counts.
The results illustrate a workflow; they are not validated sample-size
recommendations for a particular disease.

# Store genotypes and sample annotations together

Bioconductor's `SummarizedExperiment` class keeps an assay matrix together
with its sample annotations. Here rows represent variants, columns represent
individuals, the `GT` assay stores genotypes, and `colData()` stores case/control
status. Subsetting the object keeps samples and annotations aligned. The
[SummarizedExperiment introduction](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/SummarizedExperiment/inst/doc/SummarizedExperiment.html)
describes this layout in more detail.

For a diploid biallelic variant, genotype codes 0, 1, and 2 count copies of the
same specified allele in every individual. We construct 100 cases and 100
controls without random sampling, so no random seed is needed.

```{r pilot-data, message=FALSE}
library(paweh)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

case_genotypes <- rep(0:2, times = c(25, 50, 25))
control_genotypes <- rep(0:2, times = c(36, 48, 16))
sample_ids <- paste0("sample_", seq_len(200))

pilot <- SummarizedExperiment(
  assays = list(GT = matrix(
    c(case_genotypes, control_genotypes), nrow = 1,
    dimnames = list("rs_pilot", sample_ids)
  )),
  colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
    status = rep(c("case", "control"), each = 100),
    row.names = sample_ids
  )
)
table(colData(pilot)$status)
```

The resulting case frequencies are `c(0.25, 0.50, 0.25)` and control
frequencies are `c(0.36, 0.48, 0.16)`, in genotype order 0, 1, 2. The wrappers
calculate these distributions separately within the two annotated groups.
They accept both `SummarizedExperiment` and `RangedSummarizedExperiment`
objects, provided the selected assay contains numeric genotype hard calls.
Expression counts and fractional genotype dosages are not suitable inputs.

# How many participants should the new study recruit?

We select the named variant `rs_pilot`, assay `GT`, and the explicit labels
`"case"` and `"control"` in the `status` column. A target power of 0.80 means
an 80% probability of detecting an association under the assumed genotype
distributions and test. Here `k = 1` plans one control per case.

We use `alpha = 0.05` for a single prespecified primary test at one candidate
variant. Choose the threshold to match the actual testing strategy. For
example, a Bonferroni threshold for one million tests and family-wise error
rate 0.05 would be `0.05 / 1e6`, or `5e-8`; this requires recalculating the
design at that threshold. Genome-wide studies therefore should not reuse
the sample sizes below with an unadjusted 0.05 threshold. The R
[multiple-comparison documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html)
describes common adjustment methods.

`paweh` reports two alternatives: the **genotype test** compares all three
genotype proportions (two degrees of freedom); the **trend test** looks for
a change with allele count, using default scores `c(0, 1, 2)` (one degree of
freedom). Choose the primary test before the new study. If both are used as
confirmatory tests, the significance strategy must account for both tests as
well as the variants examined.

```{r required-sample-size, comment=NA}
sample_size <- cc_mssn_from_se(
  se = pilot, variant = "rs_pilot", assay_name = "GT",
  group_col = "status", case_value = "case", control_value = "control",
  power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, k = 1,
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

The genotype test requires **`r sample_size$tests$genotypes$MSSN_case` cases
and `r sample_size$tests$genotypes$MSSN_ctrl` controls**
(`r sample_size$tests$genotypes$MSSN_total` participants in total).
The trend test requires **`r sample_size$tests$trend$MSSN_case` cases and
`r sample_size$tests$trend$MSSN_ctrl` controls**
(`r sample_size$tests$trend$MSSN_total` total). These are separate designs for
the two tests, not numbers to add together. The trend test needs fewer
participants for this particular contrast; that is not a general guarantee.
The counts are rounded up to whole participants and do not include an
allowance for dropout or unusable future samples.

# What power would a proposed sample size provide?

Suppose the team can recruit 250 new cases and 250 new controls. Although
the pilot contains only 100 participants per group, `N_case = 250` and `k = 1`
specify the future study. The pilot supplies frequencies, not recruitment
counts.

```{r proposed-study-power, comment=NA}
planned_power <- cc_power_from_se(
  se = pilot, variant = "rs_pilot", assay_name = "GT",
  group_col = "status", case_value = "case", control_value = "control",
  N_case = 250, alpha = 0.05, k = 1,
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

Under these assumptions, power is approximately
**`r round(100 * planned_power$tests$genotypes$power, 1)`% for the genotype
test** and **`r round(100 * planned_power$tests$trend$power, 1)`% for the trend
test**. Both exceed the 80% target. Changing the allocation ratio, threshold,
or assumed genotype frequencies changes these calculations.

# The same calculation with explicit frequencies

The wrappers are convenience interfaces to the existing statistical engines.
To see this, count the genotypes in each pilot group, divide by the number of
usable calls, and supply the frequencies directly to `cc_mssn()`. The three
bins preserve genotype order even if a genotype is absent.

```{r manual-frequency-comparison}
genotypes <- assay(pilot, "GT")["rs_pilot", ]
status <- colData(pilot)$status
cases <- genotypes[status == "case" & !is.na(genotypes)]
controls <- genotypes[status == "control" & !is.na(genotypes)]
g1 <- tabulate(cases + 1L, nbins = 3L) / length(cases)
g0 <- tabulate(controls + 1L, nbins = 3L) / length(controls)

manual_sample_size <- cc_mssn(
  power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, input_mode = "model_free",
  g1 = g1, g0 = g0, k = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
identical(sample_size, manual_sample_size)
```

`TRUE` confirms that the complete returned objects agree, including both
tests. `verbose = FALSE` suppresses the formatted summary while retaining
the structured result, returned invisibly for assignment or further use.

# Interpret pilot-based designs cautiously

Pilot frequencies are estimates, and small samples can give imprecise or
overstated contrasts, especially if a variant was selected because it looked
promising in that pilot. These calculations treat the supplied frequencies
as fixed; they do not propagate their estimation uncertainty. Compare
plausible frequency scenarios and consider independent evidence before
choosing a recruitment target.

The wrappers exclude missing genotype calls separately within each group and
require usable calls in both groups. Missing group labels and samples outside
the selected labels are excluded. Missing calls can bias the estimated
frequencies when some genotypes are more likely to be missing within a group.
Genotype quality, consistent allele coding, and relevance of the pilot
population to the future study therefore matter.

The wrappers perform prospective design calculations, not association tests
on the pilot data. Calculating observed post hoc power from the same completed
study is not their intended use. Their purpose here is to plan a new,
independent follow-up study under explicitly stated assumptions.
